advisor.summary: For a multi-owner business, partnership versus S corporation is a five-axis trade — and only one axis favors the S corporation: employment tax. An S owner pays FICA on reasonable W-2 compensation and takes the balance as distributions, while a general partner's guaranteed payments and distributive share are generally swept into self-employment income — and after Renkemeyer and Soroban, the limited-partner exclusion is contested ground for active LLC members. Nearly every other axis runs the opposite way: §704(b) special allocations, outside basis from entity-level debt under §752, inside-basis step-ups through the §754/§743(b) machinery, tax-free movement of property in and out, and freedom from the single-class-of-stock straitjacket. The answer is fact-driven — service firms with pro-rata owners usually take the S corporation's payroll savings; leveraged real estate and unequal-economics deals usually need the partnership. This record frames the decision; once the choice tilts toward S, the S-corp election strategy models the employment-tax dollars.
mechanics: Employment tax is the S corporation's axis: only reasonable W-2 compensation bears FICA and distributions escape it, while a partner's guaranteed payments under §707(c) and distributive share of business income are generally self-employment income under §1402(a) — and Rev. Rul. 69-184 forecloses treating a partner as a W-2 employee of the partnership at all.

The §1402(a)(13) limited-partner exclusion is the contested seam: Renkemeyer put active service partners outside it, Soroban made 'limited partner' status a question of functional analysis rather than state-law labeling and applied that test against the active partners on the merits in 2025, and the appellate courts are now split — the Fifth Circuit sided with the state-law label in Sirius Solutions (2026) while Soroban's appeal awaits the Second Circuit — never promise SE savings inside a partnership to an active member.

Allocations are the partnership's axis: §704(b) respects disproportionate splits of income, loss, and cash that carry substantial economic effect — preferred returns, waterfalls, sweat-equity deals — while the S corporation's single-class-of-stock rule holds every owner to strict pro-rata sharing.

Debt basis separates the forms decisively in leveraged ventures: partnership liabilities enter outside basis under §752, supporting losses and debt-financed distributions, while S shareholders build basis only from stock and direct shareholder loans under §1366(d) — entity-level bank debt gives them nothing.

The §754 election unlocks §743(b) inside-basis adjustments when interests transfer by sale or death — effectively fresh depreciation for the buyer or heir — and appreciated property generally enters under §721 and exits under §731 tax-free, while an S corporation recognizes gain when it distributes appreciated property under §311(b).

Guaranteed payments are the partnership's compensation dial: fixed, deductible amounts set by agreement with no reasonableness exam standard — but fully SE-taxed and excluded from the recipient's QBI under Reg. §1.199A-3, so the §199A price of that flexibility has to be counted.

S-shareholder loss limits: stock basis plus direct shareholder loans, nothing more.

requirements: Two or more genuine co-owners — the comparison exists only for real multi-owner ventures.
For the S route: continuous §1361 eligibility — eligible shareholders, one class of stock, the shareholder cap — which by itself rules out many deal structures.
For the partnership route: an operating or partnership agreement built to §704(b) standards, with capital-account maintenance and guaranteed-payment terms set deliberately.
Willingness to carry the chosen form's compliance load: reasonable-compensation support for S corporations, K-1 and capital-account complexity for partnerships.
risks: The partnership's recurring cost is SE tax on active members' full shares, and the aggressive answer — claiming the limited-partner exclusion while running the business — is precisely what Renkemeyer and Soroban Capital Partners punish; the Tax Court held against Soroban's partners on the merits in 2025, and although the Fifth Circuit ruled for the taxpayer in Sirius Solutions (2026), the resulting circuit split — with the Soroban appeal pending in the Second Circuit — keeps this an actively litigated position, not a planning default.

The S corporation's mirror-image exposure is reasonable compensation: David E. Watson, P.C. v. United States, 668 F.3d 1008 (8th Cir. 2012), recharacterized low wages — the payroll savings cannot be manufactured by zeroing out the salary.

Choosing S for the payroll savings and later needing preferred returns, investor classes, or waterfalls the single-class-of-stock rule forbids is the classic expensive regret — conversions out are not free, and appreciated assets leave an S corporation only with gain recognition.
Inadvertent S termination — a side agreement creating a second class of stock, or an ineligible shareholder arriving through death or trust funding — destroys the election retroactively.
Partnership complexity is a real cost: §704(c) layers, capital accounts, and liability recomputations add preparation cost and error risk every year.
stateNotes: Conformity: Missouri conforms to the federal characterization of both forms through its federal starting point, so the federal analysis carries onto the state return without adjustment.

PTET interaction: neutral between the forms in Missouri — the SALT Parity Act election (RSMo §143.436) is open to both S corporations and partnerships, so the entity-level deduction survives whichever form wins.

Missouri: no separate state election mechanics distinguish the forms, so the Missouri decision rides entirely on the federal axes — employment tax, allocations, debt basis, step-ups, and property movement.

client.teaser: Partnership or S corporation? The choice is worth real money every year — and the answer depends on how your business runs.
client.headline: Two ways to structure a co-owned business — priced side by side
plainEnglish: When a business has more than one owner, there are two main tax setups: a partnership or an S corporation. From the outside they look alike — both pass profits straight to the owners' returns. But they behave very differently, and the wrong pick costs money every year.

The S corporation usually wins on payroll taxes. You take a fair salary, and profits above it skip the extra 15% tax. The trade-off is rigid rules: every owner must share profits exactly by ownership share, no exceptions.

A partnership flips that. Owners can split profits and cash almost any way they agree. One owner can draw a fixed payment for their work. Business loans can unlock extra deductions for the owners. The trade-off is more payroll-style tax for working owners.

Neither is simply better. If the business runs on the owners' work, the S corporation often wins. If it runs on property, debt, or uneven deals between owners, the partnership often wins. We price both with your real numbers before anything is filed.
client.analogy: It is like choosing between a sedan and a pickup. The sedan costs less to run each day. But if your life involves hauling, the truck earns its keep. The mistake is buying on sticker price without looking at your driveway.
benefits: A structure matched to how your business actually makes money
Payroll-tax savings when the S corporation route fits
Freedom to split profits unevenly and reward sweat equity when the partnership fits
Fewer costly do-overs when investors, property, or heirs enter the picture
steps: WE map how your business earns money, borrows, and pays its owners.

YOU and your co-owners choose the winner with us and sign the updated agreement.
